title: Take Five: Five Takeaways from Daniel Willingham's Close Look at Comprehension
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Harriett Janetos organizes a discussion of reading comprehension with Daniel Willingham on The Literacy View podcast into five takeaways, interleaving transcript excerpts with her own framing and related research. The first is that knowledge drives comprehension, because a reader who lacks background has no cognitive effort left for higher-level thought. The second concerns how to teach knowledge across the ELA, science and social studies blocks without crowding out content time, with the fourth-grade slump as a warning. The third and fourth cover coordinating and monitoring meaning, where students who only check that they decoded words fail to tie sentences together. The fifth reviews strategy instruction: it helps, is learned quickly, and delivers a one-time boost that should be a small part of a teacher's job. Janetos closes with the Willingham and Hirsch claim that broad vocabulary and background knowledge yield the larger long-term gains.
points: Background knowledge is the workhorse of comprehension, since a reader struggling with the bare who, what and where has no capacity left to think about motives or ideas.
The fourth-grade slump is best explained as a hidden knowledge gap that tests only expose once decoding is fluent, so crowding out science and social studies for foundational skills backfires later.
Students often monitor whether they said the words right rather than whether the text makes sense, so teachers need to explicitly teach monitoring for meaning.
Comprehension strategies are quick to learn and give a one-time boost, so they deserve modest instructional time compared with building vocabulary and knowledge.
Knowledge versus strategies is a false dichotomy, because children need knowledge to make meaning and also need to know how to recruit it while reading.
quotes: All of the things that we hope for in children as a product of schooling—creative thinking, effective problem solving, wise decision making—all of these skills that we want to build for students don’t stand alone.
So if I’m struggling just to figure out the bare bones—who, what, where, why, when—there’s no room, there’s no cognitive effort left for me to think at a higher level.
You have children reading on grade level and then all of a sudden at fourth grade, they fall off the table. And Chall, I think, correctly diagnosed that as a background knowledge problem.
That’s what I think is missing in a lot of classrooms: teaching kids, and that comes back to that explicit instruction, how to monitor for meaning.
Teaching reading strategies is a low-cost way to give developing readers a boost, but it should be a small part of a teacher’s job.
If you’re missing the background knowledge, there’s not a strategy that is going to put that knowledge in its place.
